rationale: The paper is a small-molecule homogeneous organic reaction study of N-cyclopropyl MPTP analogues oxidized by 3-methyllumiflavin under photochemical biomimetic conditions. The authors performed and reported non-routine molecular-orbital calculations directly addressing the reaction phenomenon: ring opening versus ring closure of the radical cations generated from 4a, cis-4b, trans-4b, and trans-4c, including cis/trans isomerization for the methyl-substituted case. Experimental observations in CD3CN under anaerobic/aerobic photochemical conditions provide public starting context, while the computed barriers and reaction energies are private evaluation references. No critical identity or result gap prevents formulating a bounded research question.

source_quotes.quote: The reactions of 3MLF with N-cyclopropyl MPTP derivatives { \bf 4 } \left( { \bf a } { - } { \bf c } \right) were studied under anaerobic and aerobic conditions. The reactions were monitored by <sup>1</sup>H NMR. The solvent was \mathrm { C D } _ { 3 } \mathrm { C N } . . This solvent contained a small amount of _ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } } which proved critical in the analysis of the outcomes of these experiments. The reactions were typically performed on a 2−5 mM scale. The ratio of 3MLF to substrate was as close to 1:1 as feasible. NMR spectra were recorded at t = 0 and after the reaction had gone to completion (20−24 h).

For reactions conducted under anaerobic conditions, the final NMR spectra were obtained before and after exposure to air and, in some cases, benzene was added as an internal standard. The reaction mixtures were further analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Volatile products (low molecular weight aldehydes) were separated by a room temperature trap-to-trap distillation using a vacuum line and analyzed by NMR. A reviewer commented favorably that these complex reaction mixtures were analyzed as fully as possible given the constraints, \mathbf { e . g . } , the small scale of the reactions dictated by the limited availability of the tetrahydropyridine derivatives, and concerns about their potential neurotoxicity.

Unlike our earlier results for the reaction of 3MLF with \mathbf { M M T P } _ { \mathrm { , } } ^ { 2 0 } the reactions of all the N-cyclopropyl MPTP derivatives with 3MLF required visible light (50 W tungsten light bulb). There was no significant thermal reaction detected within a 24 h period in the dark. The low energy excited states of 3MLF have a redox potential \left( E _ { 1 / 2 } \mathrm { ( t r i p l e t ) } \ = \ 2 . 1 \right. A detailed analysis of the results for the reaction of 3MLF and 4a is provided below. Results for 4b and 4c are available in the Supporting Information. Molecular orbital calculations were performed to support and amplify these findings.

The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum for the reaction of a 1:1 mix of 3MLF and 4a after 20 h of irradiation under anaerobic conditions is shown in Figure 6. Figure 6a is the spectrum obtained after the reaction is complete and still under anaerobic conditions. Most of the peaks in this spectrum can be assigned to either unreacted substrate (4a) or products \bf ( 5 a - 8 a ) , based upon direct comparison to authentic spectra. Most notably though, no peaks associated with 3MLF are observed and there are a few unassigned peaks, presumed to arise from reaction intermediates (noted in dotted rectangular boxes). When the NMR tube was opened and exposed to air, peaks attributable to 3MLF reappeared while the unknown peaks vanished (Figure 6b). LC-MS/MS analysis of the reaction mixture detected only 4a, 5a, \mathbf { 6 , } and 3MLF. Finally, the volatile components of the reaction mixture, propionaldehyde (7a) and propenal (8a) were separated by high vacuum trap-to-trap distillation at room temperature and their identities were further confirmed by <sup>1</sup>H NMR analysis. In response to a reviewer comment, it should be noted that the volatile aldehydes could not be resolved from solvent by GC or HPLC. However, the fact that they were in fact volatile (separated by ambient temperature vacuum distillation), and the NMR spectra matched authentic samples leaves no ambiguity as to the assignment.

The results for the reactions of 3MLF with 4b and 4c were similar and are summarized in Table 2. In all cases, there was approximately 50% unreacted substrate, which is consistent with the reaction stoichiometry (vide infra). Two products derived from the tetrahydropyridine moiety of the substrate were observed, a pyridinium species which maintained a closed cyclopropane ring (5), and 4-phenylpyridine (6).

Compounds 6−8 likely arise from cyclopropane ring opening, as shown in Figure 7. Ring opening of radical cation 4 ^ { \hat { \bullet } + } leads to distonic radical cation { \hat { \mathbf { g ^ { \bullet + } } } } , which can undergo disproportionation leading to 10 and 11 (precursors to 7 and 8). Alternatively, there is also another possible H atom donor present, namely the substrate itself. The calculations for 4 \mathbf { b } ^ { \bullet ^ { + } } are particularly noteworthy. For the cis isomer, there is a low barrier to ring opening, and the overall process is favorable. Overall, for the reaction of compounds _ { 4 ( \mathsf { a } - \mathsf { c } ) } with 3MLF, the amount of ring opened products observed seems unrelated to rate of ring opening. We believe that the reason for this is that { \mathfrak { s } } ( { \mathfrak { a } } { - } { \mathfrak { c } } ) are not formed as a result of the competition depicted in Figure ^ { 3 , } but rather, as a consequence of the hydrogen atom abstraction from substrate described above as shown in Figure 11. The substrate radical generated from this process is readily oxidized under the reaction conditions, providing a pathway for the formation of a fully oxidized product with the cyclopropyl group intact because a radical is never generated in the vicinity of the cyclopropyl moiety.

Finally, these reactions of 3MLF and 4 (a−c) were also performed under aerobic conditions. The mass balance for 4a was poor (because of overoxidation), but 4b and 4c provided useful new information. For 4b, the results were essentially the same as observed anaerobically in terms of the production of 5 and 6. The diference was that rather than butyraldehyde (7b), a diferent aldehyde was produced (acetaldehyde, in addition to 8b). Similarly, for reaction of _ { 4 \mathrm { c } , } benzaldehyde was produced in lieu of { 7 } \mathbf { c } . These new products are clearly the result of trapping of the ring-opened distonic radical cations by \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } , with subsequent decomposition of the resulting peroxides via classical free radical pathways (Figure 12). For all these
aerobic reactions, 3MLF was continuously regenerated by \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } and catalytic in the production of the various aldehydes (pertinent spectra are provided in the Supporting Information).

All chemicals and solvents used were at the highest purity available. Details of the synthesis of 3-methyllumiflavin (3MLF) can be found in the work originally reported by Ghisla et al.<sup>37</sup> All MPTP derivatives were synthesized according to literature procedures and stored as their respective oxalate or hydrochloride salts: 4a,<sup>38</sup> cis-4b,<sup>32</sup> trans- \mathbf { 4 c } , ^ { 3 2 } and 4 \mathrm { a } _ { \mathrm { D } 4 } . ^ { 3 } 9 The salts were treated using aqueous potassium carbonate solutions and the generated free amine was extracted using methylene chloride.

NMR spectra were recorded using a Bruker Neo400HT NMR (400 MHz). Data analyses were performed using MestreNova. All reactions were prepared using degassed CD CN stock solutions. Stocks were kept refrigerated unless being actively used. This was done primarily to maintain consistency in sample preparation. Aerobic reactions were prepared directly in NMR tubes with a total reaction volume of approximately 0.6 mL. To ensure proper and consistent aeration of the sample, the tubes were placed on a mixing table when not being analyzed. Anaerobic reactions were also prepared directly in NMR tubes, but were immediately freeze−pump−thaw degassed (the process started <1 min after mixing). After degassing, the NMR tubes were flame-sealed. The reaction mixtures were irradiated with a 50W tungsten lamp from a distance of ca. 1−2 feet.

scientific_question: For the photochemically generated N-cyclopropyl 1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine radical cations derived from the MPTP-related substrates with cyclopropyl substituents R = H, Me, and Ph, how does the cyclopropyl substituent control the relative accessibility of cyclopropane ring opening versus retention of the ring-closed framework, and how does this behavior differ between the cis and trans methyl-substituted radical cations under the reported acetonitrile biomimetic oxidation conditions?
computation_relevance: The question is directly supported by the authors' reported molecular-orbital calculations of ring-opening barriers and reaction energies for the radical cations generated from 4(a-c), plus the reported inability to locate a ring-closed minimum for trans-4c radical cation. These computations address the same chemical behavior asked in the question: substituent-dependent competition between ring opening and ring-closed retention, including cis/trans effects for the methyl-substituted case. The experimental reaction data provide context for the conditions and observed products, but the computed barriers and energetics are the private references for evaluating the question.

source_quotes.quote: The first issue to address regarding these results is why do these reactions require light? Earlier work demonstrated a thermal reaction between 3MLF and MMTP.<sup>20</sup> We believe the diference is attributable to the fact that MMTP is much more easily oxidized than MPTP and any of its N-cyclopropyl derivatives. To test this, calculations were performed to assess energetics of a hypothetical electron transfer between the 1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridinyl radical cation and MPTP, MMTP, and related compounds. The results, summarized in Table ^ { 1 , } reveal that MMTP is more readily oxidized than MPTP by 500 mV. The results also show that the phenyl group in MPTP has little efect on the oxidation energetics ( \Delta E ~ < 100 mV, comparing MPTP to 1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine). Thus, MPTP derivatives require a substantially more potent oxidant ( \mathrm { i . e . , } the excited state of 3 \mathbf { M L F } ) ^ { 2 6 } to drive the electron transfer process.

public_inputs.content: The reaction system involves N-cyclopropyl analogues of 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine with cyclopropyl substituents R = H, Me, and Ph, corresponding to substrates 4a, 4b, and 4c in the source. The methyl-substituted substrate 4b is considered in both cis and trans forms.

source_quotes.quote: Figure 4. (a) Mechanism-based MAO inhibitors used by Silverman<sup>7,8,23</sup> and Castagnoli<sup>10,11,24</sup> to probe for single electron transfer. (b) N-Cyclopropyl analogs of MPTP used in this study.

The present work examines the chemistry of several 3 ^ { \circ } Ncyclopropyl compounds related to MPTP in a biomimetic system (Figure 4b) with a focus on the chemistry that occurs after single electron transfer. The principal objectives are to determine whether ring opening occurs, and if so, to identify the resulting products. We hypothesize that these results will provide new insight into the mechanism of MAO-catalyzed oxidations, especially in the context of enzyme inactivation. As noted, for the SET probe approach to succeed, ring opening should be rapid and irreversible, and this study will test these assumptions.

The reactions of 3MLF with N-cyclopropyl MPTP derivatives { \bf 4 } \left( { \bf a } { - } { \bf c } \right) were studied under anaerobic and aerobic conditions. The reactions were monitored by <sup>1</sup>H NMR. The solvent was \mathrm { C D } _ { 3 } \mathrm { C N } . . This solvent contained a small amount of _ { \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } } which proved critical in the analysis of the outcomes of these experiments. The reactions were typically performed on a 2−5 mM scale. The ratio of 3MLF to substrate was as close to 1:1 as feasible. NMR spectra were recorded at t = 0 and after the reaction had gone to completion (20−24 h).

The results for the reactions of 3MLF with 4b and 4c were similar and are summarized in Table 2. NMR spectra were recorded using a Bruker Neo400HT NMR (400 MHz). Data analyses were performed using MestreNova. All reactions were prepared using degassed CD CN stock solutions. Stocks were kept refrigerated unless being actively used. This was done primarily to maintain consistency in sample preparation. Aerobic reactions were prepared directly in NMR tubes with a total reaction volume of approximately 0.6 mL. To ensure proper and consistent aeration of the sample, the tubes were placed on a mixing table when not being analyzed. Anaerobic reactions were also prepared directly in NMR tubes, but were immediately freeze−pump−thaw degassed (the process started <1 min after mixing). After degassing, the NMR tubes were flame-sealed. The reaction mixtures were irradiated with a 50W tungsten lamp from a distance of ca. 1−2 feet.

public_inputs.content: Under anaerobic photochemical reaction conditions, the authors observed mixtures containing unreacted substrate, a ring-closed pyridinium product retaining the cyclopropane ring, 4-phenylpyridine, and low-molecular-weight aldehydes; exposure to oxygen changed the product distribution and regenerated 3MLF.

source_quotes.quote: The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum for the reaction of a 1:1 mix of 3MLF and 4a after 20 h of irradiation under anaerobic conditions is shown in Figure 6. Figure 6a is the spectrum obtained after the reaction is complete and still under anaerobic conditions. Most of the peaks in this spectrum can be assigned to either unreacted substrate (4a) or products \bf ( 5 a - 8 a ) , based upon direct comparison to authentic spectra. Most notably though, no peaks associated with 3MLF are observed and there are a few unassigned peaks, presumed to arise from reaction intermediates (noted in dotted rectangular boxes). When the NMR tube was opened and exposed to air, peaks attributable to 3MLF reappeared while the unknown peaks vanished (Figure 6b). LC-MS/MS analysis of the reaction mixture detected only 4a, 5a, \mathbf { 6 , } and 3MLF. Finally, the volatile components of the reaction mixture, propionaldehyde (7a) and propenal (8a) were separated by high vacuum trap-to-trap distillation at room temperature and their identities were further confirmed by <sup>1</sup>H NMR analysis. In response to a reviewer comment, it should be noted that the volatile aldehydes could not be resolved from solvent by GC or HPLC. However, the fact that they were in fact volatile (separated by ambient temperature vacuum distillation), and the NMR spectra matched authentic samples leaves no ambiguity as to the assignment.

The results for the reactions of 3MLF with 4b and 4c were similar and are summarized in Table 2. In all cases, there was approximately 50% unreacted substrate, which is consistent with the reaction stoichiometry (vide infra). Two products derived from the tetrahydropyridine moiety of the substrate were observed, a pyridinium species which maintained a closed cyclopropane ring (5), and 4-phenylpyridine (6).

Compounds 6−8 likely arise from cyclopropane ring opening, as shown in Figure 7. Ring opening of radical cation 4 ^ { \hat { \bullet } + } leads to distonic radical cation { \hat { \mathbf { g ^ { \bullet + } } } } , which can undergo disproportionation leading to 10 and 11 (precursors to 7 and 8). Alternatively, there is also another possible H atom donor present, namely the substrate itself. The \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } moiety in the substrate that is α-both to nitrogen and the { \mathrm { C } } { = } { \dot { \mathrm { C } } } has an unusually low C−H bond dissociation energy (75 kcal/mol).<sup>21</sup> Hydrolysis of the iminium species by \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } (present in the CD CN NMR solvent) generates the observed aldehydes.

As noted earlier, when the anaerobic reactions of 1:1 3MLF:4(a−c) were analyzed by NMR, no peaks associated with 3MLF were observed and there are a few unknown peaks (noted in the dotted rectangular boxes in Figure 6). In all these reactions, the major products were a cyclopropane ring closed pyridinium species (5), 4-phenylpyridine (6), low molecular weight aldehydes (7 and 8), and about 50% unreacted substrate (4). When the NMR tube was opened and exposed to oxygen, peaks attributable to 3MLF reappeared while the unknown peaks vanished while some of the known peaks increased in intensity. The 1:1 ratio of reactants proved critical in revealing some of the nuances associated with these reactions, \mathbf { e . g . } _ { } , cis/trans isomerization of 4b, which would have been missed if the reactions had gone to completion.

Finally, these reactions of 3MLF and 4 (a−c) were also performed under aerobic conditions. The mass balance for 4a was poor (because of overoxidation), but 4b and 4c provided useful new information. For 4b, the results were essentially the same as observed anaerobically in terms of the production of 5 and 6. The diference was that rather than butyraldehyde (7b), a diferent aldehyde was produced (acetaldehyde, in addition to 8b). Similarly, for reaction of _ { 4 \mathrm { c } , } benzaldehyde was produced in lieu of { 7 } \mathbf { c } . These new products are clearly the result of trapping of the ring-opened distonic radical cations by \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } , with subsequent decomposition of the resulting peroxides via classical free radical pathways (Figure 12). For all these
aerobic reactions, 3MLF was continuously regenerated by \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } and catalytic in the production of the various aldehydes (pertinent spectra are provided in the Supporting Information).

public_inputs.content: For cis-4b, the authors observed cis/trans isomerization during the reaction by comparison of cyclopropyl-region 1H NMR spectra at t = 0 and t = 20 h.

source_quotes.quote: As noted in the introduction, the use of N-cyclopropyl substrates as probes for single electron transfer is predicated on the assumption that, in analogy to the cyclopropylcarbinyl → homoallyl neutral radical rearrangement, ring opening is rapid and essentially irreversible. These calculations reveal that this may only hold true for 4 c ^ { \bullet + } . For 4 \mathbf { a } ^ { \bullet + } , calculations indicate that ring opening may be slow and thermodynamically unfavorable. The calculations for 4 \mathbf { b } ^ { \bullet ^ { + } } are particularly noteworthy. For the cis isomer, there is a low barrier to ring opening, and the overall process is favorable. Ring opening of the trans isomer has a higher barrier and is unfavorable. More importantly, the ringclosed trans form of 4 \mathbf { b } ^ { \bullet + } is lower in energy than either c i s \mathbf { - } 4 \mathbf { b } ^ { \mathbf { \tilde { \bullet } } + } (ring closed) or any of the ring opened structures. This prediction is supported by the experimental results, because if one looks carefully at the cyclopropyl region of the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra before ( t \overset { \cdot } { = } 0 ) and after reaction \mathbf { \bar { \rho } } ( t = 2 0 \ \mathrm { h } ) . , it is clear that a significant amount of the starting material has undergone cis → trans isomerization during the course of the reaction (Figure 10). The results clearly demonstrate that while ring opening of cis-4b<sup>•+</sup> may be favorable, the lowest energy product that arises from that process is trans-4b<sup>•+</sup> and not the ring opened products.

Figure 10. <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra of the cyclopropyl region from the reaction of 3MLF and cis-4b in CD CN at (a) t = 0, and (b) t = 20 h. The labeled peaks show the position of the (clearly resolved) cyclopropyl hydrogens of the starting material, and demonstrate that cis/trans isomerization occurred during the course of the reaction. Cis/trans assignments were based upon <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra of the pure compounds (see Supporting Information). Figure 11. Substrate radical generated by hydrogen atom abstraction can undergo further oxidation leading to a pyridinium ion with the cyclopropyl group intact.

reference_limitations: The reported computational values are electronic-energy differences from molecular-orbital calculations, not experimental free energies or rate constants.
The authors report that values vary somewhat with method and basis set, although trends are described as consistent; no uncertainty estimates are provided.
The calculations are for isolated radical-cation model systems and do not include explicit solvent, counterions, light absorption, or the full 3MLF reaction environment.
The public question should not require reproducing the authors' exact conformational labels or mechanism; those labels are private references for comparison.
